Inside, huge 12-foot west-facing windows rise into a double-height room crossed by the bank's original symmetrical steel A-frame truss, with a mezzanine balcony and a quieter area beneath it. A communal table sits by the entrance, a long bar with shoulder-height panels and booths line the room, and an open kitchen with a wood-fired oven anchors the back, while Brian Barneclo's cartoonish San Francisco murals cover the entrance wall and the wall above the mezzanine.
placeResearch.unique: The exposed steel A-frame truss and double-height volume left from the old bank, whose former vault is still used for storage.

placeResearch.street: Mid-block storefront at 2340 Polk Street between Union and Green in Russian Hill, on Polk's neighborhood shopping strip, with a few tables on the sidewalk.

The exterior is painted charcoal grey, with a large picture window on the left bearing hand-painted gold-leaf lettering, a recessed glass door on the right and a bar-height window counter. Inside, white upper walls under four skylights meet engineered white-oak paneling that runs at an angle across floor and walls, with a bar faced in matte white hexagonal tile under a white quartz top, bent unfinished-steel shelving, a 20-foot solid wood bench and a rear mezzanine.

placeResearch.street: Storefront on Columbus Avenue at Vallejo Street in North Beach, in business here since the early 1900s, a short walk from Caffe Trieste on Vallejo and two blocks from Washington Square. A few small tables sit on the sidewalk out front.
placeResearch.terrain: Level ground in the North Beach valley between Telegraph Hill and Russian Hill. Looking south down diagonal Columbus Avenue, the Transamerica Pyramid is visible in the distance.
placeResearch.architecture: Old-fashioned Italian delicatessen storefront with a sign and a striped awning over the entrance, reportedly blue and white. Inside is a narrow, crowded shop with wooden floors, vintage photographs, floor-to-ceiling shelves of imported tins and jars, glass deli cases and a counter at the back.

Upstairs is the main dining room, open to a kitchen with custom stainless-steel work; downstairs is a small bar with about ten seats and two tables. places.summary: A Parisian-style wine bar and shop from the team behind Quince and Cotogna.

placeResearch.street: Corner of Washington Street and Hotaling Place, a one-block lane called San Francisco's oldest alley, in the Jackson Square historic district, directly across Washington from the Transamerica Pyramid. It fills two joined storefronts.

placeResearch.architecture: Ground floor of the 1850s brick building known as the "Eclipse Champagne Building", its street windows fitted with vintage mahogany louvers on pivots. The interior, by Jensen Architects, has a 14-foot ceiling in high-gloss burgundy lacquer, white-painted original masonry walls, a seven-shade Spanish encaustic cement tile floor and an ebonized wood and black slate bar. A backlit movie-marquee-style menu board hangs over the open kitchen counter, among elm millwork and asymmetrical shelving, Pierre Chapo elm tables and chairs, an 1890s apothecary cabinet and rolling glass doors between rooms.
placeResearch.unique: The glossy burgundy lacquered ceiling, applied in ten coats and inspired by the Paris wine bar Le Baron Rouge, glows orange by candlelight.

placeResearch.street: Stall inside the Ferry Building Marketplace on the Embarcadero, in the long central nave between Lunette and Village Market, on the south hall's Bay side, in the space formerly held by SF Fish Company. Two long wooden communal tables on wheels sit at the edge of the hall.

The counter and walls are covered in deep-blue handmade tile by Georgia Hodges, with an eight-foot glass market case, about 100 small ceramic fish hung above the refrigerated case and register, and hand-painted signage by David Benzler. Seating is about 28, mostly at two long custom wooden communal tables on casters.

Huge street windows face Columbus, and each entrance has a custom floor tile mosaic; signage uses custom letterforms inspired by mid-century Italian type in a terra cotta palette. Kitchen prep areas sit at the street windows, and on the plaza a glassed-in, greenhouse-style dining room now sits under a heated canopy with permanent planters.

placeResearch.architecture: A narrow storefront given a new brick front in its 2012 build-out, with a big black awning over the sidewalk and neon signage that makes it hard to miss at night; heavy front doors lead into a long, narrow, dimly lit room. Inside are exposed century-old Chicago brick walls (about seven tons), a hand-painted pressed-tin ceiling, cork floors, curved oxblood tufted booths, and an Art Deco-inspired mahogany bar modeled on the Golden Gate Bridge with a restored 1937 brass National cash register at its center. A working 1930s phone booth sits at the back, vintage hubcaps and mob-era photos line the walls, and a restored 1960s panoramic painting of the space's former Adolf Restaurant, found in the floorboards, hangs above the Capone booth.
placeResearch.unique: A Prohibition-era Chicago stage set built new in 2012: seven tons of reclaimed Chicago brick, booths named for Chicago mobsters, a free-call phone booth, and a rediscovered 1960s mural of the room's earlier restaurant.

placeResearch.street: Mid-block on Stockton Street in North Beach, near the Union Street corner and a short walk from Washington Square, in a dense row of ground-floor bars and restaurants with apartments above.
placeResearch.terrain: Level North Beach valley floor between Telegraph Hill and Russian Hill, on a narrow, busy commercial street. Since its 2023 restoration the neon sign lights up Stockton and is visible from blocks away in either direction.
placeResearch.architecture: Ground-floor bar in a multi-story mixed-use building the Nicco family bought in the 1910s, living in the apartment upstairs above what began as a French laundry. The narrow front is a green door with a cloudy, submarine-style round porthole window next to a curved wall of glass block, under a vintage neon sign hanging above the door, one of the oldest signs in North Beach ("NIK'S" was once painted over the original "NICCO'S"; the sign was restored and relit in 2023). Inside, the 1949 remodel survives: a long J-shaped bar under a stylish bar canopy, a wall of checkerboard wooden tiles, and a Nadine Torrance mural in maroon, brown and dark green covering the entire back wall.
placeResearch.unique: A rare intact 1949 bar interior (checkerboard wood-tile wall, bar canopy, full-wall mural) behind an original neon sign, preserved in a city-recognized Legacy Business open since 1933.

places.signatureRationale: Imbibe and official site: twice-yearly conceptual menus are the bar’s signature—not one permanent drink.

placeResearch.street: On 20th Street near Florida Street in the northeast Mission's former light-industrial blocks, sandwiched between the Sightglass building and Penny Roma. True Laurel and Farmhouse Kitchen are within a block.
placeResearch.terrain: Flat eastern Mission street grid of warehouses and low commercial buildings. Afternoon light pours in through the bar's lofty warehouse windows.
placeResearch.architecture: A two-level converted warehouse (The Bon Vivants Design-Build with Wylie Price Design) behind a seemingly unassuming exterior with large multi-pane industrial windows. Inside are high ceilings with turn-of-the-century Carnegie steel beams and wooden rafters strung with clear Edison bulbs, steel-framed lights salvaged from the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard, iron and wire glass, and a bar of century-old white and gray marble trimmed with banister posts and cast iron from the Warfield Building staircase. A mezzanine with a rosy-pink SEMCO floor, vintage Steelcase chairs and custom sconces made from vintage shade-cutters overlooks the main bar.
placeResearch.unique: The back bar uses a first-of-its-kind multi-layer shelving system that slides sideways on tracks, and the bar trim, stair banister and gray marble side-bar treads were salvaged from the old Warfield Building.

placeResearch.street: At 753 Alabama Street near the 20th Street corner in the northeast Mission, around the corner from Trick Dog and Penny Roma. A large sidewalk and parklet patio stretches along the frontage.

Gott's (opened in 2004 as Taylor's Automatic Refresher) is a sleek, urban take on a 1950s roadside stand: shiny steel, blond wood, chrome tables, handsome retro-font signage, long communal high tables with metal stools, an order counter and a separate pickup window, and a giant red neon "EAT" sign over the kitchen. Outside, a large open-air City View Patio with communal seating faces the Embarcadero, plus a smaller Bay View Patio.

placeResearch.street: On the corner of Columbus Avenue and Pacific Avenue at the base of North Beach, where Columbus's diagonal crosses the old Barbary Coast's main street at the meeting point of North Beach, Chinatown, the Financial District and Jackson Square; City Lights and Vesuvio are one block up Columbus, and the Transamerica Pyramid is visible in the distance.

placeResearch.architecture: A saloon building rebuilt after the 1906 earthquake and reopened in 1907 as the Andromeda Saloon, on a corner with big windows onto the street and stained-glass windows and a skylight restored in 1977. Inside: an 18-to-20-foot original mahogany bar with a white-tiled trough at its base, a restored tin ceiling, blue-and-white ceramic tile floor in the dining room, gilded ball-and-claw barstools, high-backed wooden booths, a small mezzanine balcony with an upright piano for live jazz, and a second parlor room with patterned wallpaper, velvet settees and a fireplace.
placeResearch.unique: Possibly the only intact tile trough running along the foot of a bar in the country, plus a 1916 punkah fan of brass and palm fronds that sweeps the ceiling on motor-driven leather belts, and a 1936 bronze statue of Emperor Norton above the bar.

placeResearch.architecture: A roughly 3,000-square-foot former gym converted in 2012-13 into an airy, spare, almost monastic room. Wall shelving holds rows of stock lined up like books on a bookshelf with prices chalked on, under 18th-century chandeliers, with a reclaimed marble bar as the focal point, a mezzanine, a communal table and an old wooden piano. Out front are a barrel used as a standing table, a small table with stools, and a small whale-shaped sign lettered "wine".
